enonce_intro_markdown: Nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) are important components in the synthesis of proteins in living organisms.

questions.corrige_markdown:
**Similarities.** Both are **nucleic acids**, **polymers of nucleotides** (each nucleotide = a pentose sugar + a phosphate group + a nitrogenous base) joined by **phosphodiester bonds** in a sugar-phosphate backbone. Both contain the bases **adenine, guanine and cytosine**, and both are involved in the synthesis of proteins.

**Differences**

| Feature | DNA | RNA |
|---|---|---|
| Sugar | **Deoxyribose** (one oxygen less on carbon 2) | **Ribose** |
| Nitrogenous bases | A, G, C and **thymine (T)** | A, G, C and **uracil (U)** in place of thymine |
| Number of strands | Usually **double-stranded**, two antiparallel chains forming a **double helix** | Usually **single-stranded** (tRNA is folded into a clover-leaf by internal base pairing) |
| Base pairing | A-T and G-C by hydrogen bonds between the two strands | A-U and G-C, only within a folded molecule or when pairing with DNA or other RNA |
| Size | Very **long** molecule (millions of nucleotide pairs) | **Short** (tens to a few thousand nucleotides) |
| Types | One type per cell | **Three main types**: messenger RNA (mRNA), transfer RNA (tRNA), ribosomal RNA (rRNA) |
| Location | **Nucleus** (chromosomes); also mitochondria and chloroplasts | Made in the nucleus (nucleolus); works in the **cytoplasm** and on **ribosomes**; also in mitochondria and chloroplasts |
| Stability | **Very stable**, as it keeps the genetic information for life | **Less stable**, mRNA is short-lived and broken down after use |
| Replication | **Self-replicates** (semi-conservative replication) | **Does not replicate itself**; is made from a DNA template by **transcription** (except in RNA viruses) |
| Function | **Stores and transmits genetic information**; carries the genes | **Carries out protein synthesis**: mRNA carries the code, tRNA brings amino acids, rRNA is a component of ribosomes |
| Amount | **Constant** in the cells of a species | **Varies** with the activity of the cell |

questions.enonce_markdown: Describe the events that occur in the translation of mRNA into polypeptides in cells. *[12 marks]* *(8, 12 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Translation** is the synthesis of a polypeptide whose amino-acid sequence is specified by the sequence of **codons** (triplets of bases) on mRNA. It takes place at the **ribosomes** in the cytoplasm (free ribosomes or ribosomes of the rough endoplasmic reticulum) after the mature mRNA has left the nucleus through a nuclear pore.

**Requirements:** mRNA, ribosomes (rRNA + proteins, with a small and a large subunit), 20 types of amino acids, tRNA molecules (one or more for each amino acid), enzymes, **ATP/GTP** and ions such as $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$.

**1. Activation of amino acids**

In the cytoplasm each amino acid is joined to the 3' end of its specific **transfer RNA** by the enzyme **aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase**, using energy from **ATP**. The tRNA carries at its other end an **anticodon**, three bases complementary to the codon of that amino acid.

**2. Initiation**

- The **small ribosomal subunit** binds to the 5' end (cap) of the mRNA and moves along it until it reaches the **start codon AUG**.
- The **initiator tRNA** carrying **methionine** (anticodon UAC) pairs with AUG.
- The **large subunit** then joins, to form the complete ribosome, with the initiator tRNA in the **P (peptidyl) site**; the **A (aminoacyl) site** is empty.

**3. Elongation (repeated for each amino acid)**

- A **second tRNA**, whose anticodon is complementary to the next codon, enters the **A site** and its anticodon pairs with the codon by **complementary base pairing** (hydrogen bonds).
- The enzyme **peptidyl transferase** (part of the large subunit) forms a **peptide bond** between the amino acid in the P site and that in the A site; the polypeptide is transferred to the tRNA in the A site.
- The ribosome **moves (translocates) one codon along the mRNA** in the 5' to 3' direction, using GTP. The tRNA in the A site, now carrying the chain, is moved into the P site, the free tRNA leaves from the exit site and returns to the cytoplasm to pick up another amino acid, and the A site is free for the next tRNA.

**4. Termination**

When a **stop codon (UAA, UAG or UGA)** reaches the A site, **no tRNA** has the matching anticodon. A **release factor** binds, the **polypeptide is released** (by hydrolysis of the bond to the last tRNA), and the ribosome **separates into its two subunits** and leaves the mRNA.

**5. After translation**

- **Many ribosomes read the same mRNA at the same time** (a **polyribosome** or polysome), so many copies of the polypeptide are made quickly.
- The polypeptide folds into its **secondary, tertiary and (for several chains) quaternary structure**, may be modified (e.g. cutting, addition of sugars or phosphate) in the rough ER and Golgi apparatus, and is used in the cell or exported.
